term: astray / deviate / detour / get off track / go off the rails
pronunciation:
astray: /əˈstreɪ/
deviate: /ˈdiviˌeɪt/
detour: /ˈdiˌtʊr/
get off track: /ɡɛt ɔf træk/
go off the rails: /ɡoʊ ɔf ðə reɪlz/
tts_text: astray. deviate. detour. get off track. go off the rails.
observed_forms: astray / deviate / detour / get off track / go off the rails

senses.definition: Away from the correct path or destination.
senses.example: The hikers went astray after missing a trail marker.

synonyms.note: also used figuratively for a plan or process

senses.definition: Away from the correct belief, plan, or standard of behavior.
senses.example: A misleading benchmark led the engineering team astray.

synonyms.note: a transparent phrase with a broader grammatical range

senses.definition: Lost or sent to the wrong place.
senses.example: My package seems to have gone astray.

senses.common_patterns: go astray; lead someone astray. Astray is an adverb; go or lead supplies the verb.

situations.situation: A discussion wanders away from its purpose.
situations.examples: “We’re getting off track.” / “We’re deviating from the topic.”
situations.guidance: Both work. Off track is conversational; deviating sounds more formal.

situations.examples: “We deviated from the plan to include the new requirements.”
situations.guidance: Deviate need not mean making a mistake. Go astray would suggest something went wrong.

situations.examples: “We had to take a detour.” / “We had to deviate from our planned route.”
situations.guidance: Both describe changing routes. Take a detour is the everyday travel expression.

situations.situation: Bad advice takes you in the wrong direction.
situations.examples: “That advice led me astray.” / “That advice got me off track.”
situations.guidance: Both can work. The first emphasizes being misled; the second emphasizes losing your intended direction.
Stronger than merely getting off topic; it suggests things became difficult to control.

comparison.note: These expressions overlap around leaving an intended direction. Get off track is an everyday default for losing focus. Deviate from describes departure from something specified, including deliberate changes. Take a detour is especially useful for an alternative route and can also describe a temporary diversion in discussion. Go astray suggests a wrong direction, an error, or something becoming lost. Go off the rails is usually a stronger, more dramatic description of things going wrong. Do not force a distinction where several choices work.

senses.definition: Depart from a route, plan, rule, or expected pattern. This can be deliberate and need not be bad.
senses.example: We deviated from the original plan to accommodate the client’s request.

antonyms.note: for following a plan or rule

senses.common_patterns: deviate from + plan, route, rule, topic.

senses.definition: An alternative or indirect route, often taken to avoid an obstacle or visit somewhere.
senses.example: We took a detour because the road was closed.

synonyms.note: not every alternative route is indirect

senses.common_patterns: take a detour; a detour around something; detour through somewhere.

senses.definition: Travel by an alternative or indirect route.
senses.example: We detoured through a nearby town.

senses.definition: Move away from the intended topic, task, or direction.
senses.example: We got off track discussing features we don’t actually need.

senses.common_patterns: get/go off track; get someone back on track.

senses.definition: Become uncontrolled or depart badly from the intended course; informal.
senses.example: The discussion went off the rails when people started trading insults.

synonyms.note: broader and less suggestive of losing control

senses.common_patterns: go off the rails; a meeting/project goes off the rails. Keep the and plural rails.
